# Observations of a fixed cover

Status: definitions and validation fixtures. No scientific cell is attached to this note. The static intersection graph and the static nerve are unchanged. The engine string stays `rrc-0.4.0`. The functions are `src/rrc/composition.py`.

The operator accepts an ordered family of blocks. A block is a set of carrier edges. The family is chosen with the carrier. It is not a state variable, and it is not required to be a partition or a tree. The present edges change. The family does not.

The usual mathematical words are not interchangeable.

- A full cover is a family whose union is the whole carrier.
- A partial family is a family whose union misses at least one carrier edge. Atlas-011 stored three omission lists on the triangle. Each omits one edge. Those lists are partial families. The stored cells were not rewritten, and this note does not rerun them.
- A partition is a full cover whose blocks are pairwise disjoint and nonempty.
- An overlapping cover is a full cover with at least one nonempty pairwise intersection.
- A nested family contains a block that properly contains another block. Equal blocks are not nested.
- A dynamically active subfamily is the subcollection of blocks that contain a present edge. It depends on the state. The block definitions do not.

Potential overlap and realised overlap are different conditions. Two blocks potentially overlap when their fixed edge sets meet. That condition does not read the present edges. Two blocks have realised overlap in a state when a shared edge is present. The three maps below do not test realised overlap. `active_intersection` and `labelled_active_blocks` join active blocks when the fixed sets meet, even if the shared edge is absent.

Intersection here means a shared carrier edge. Two blocks that share a vertex and no edge are disjoint for these maps. That is different from the line graph, which joins edges that share a vertex.

## Maps

| Map | Label | What it drops |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cover_count` | The number of present edges in each block, in cover order. | Which edges inside a block are present. |
| `active_intersection` | The bare intersection graph of the blocks that contain at least one present edge, plus the number of those blocks. | Which blocks are active, and which edges made them active. |
| `labelled_active_blocks` | The indices of the active blocks, and the pairs of those indices whose blocks share an edge. | Which edges made a block active. |

None adds a coordinate. A second application is undefined: a count tuple and an intersection graph are not covers. No encoding is added to apply the operator again.

## One path, two covers

The carrier is the four-edge path. The partition is `{{e0,e1},{e2,e3}}`. It is a full cover and a partition. The overlapping family is `{{e0,e1,e2},{e1,e2,e3}}`. It is a full overlapping cover, and it is not nested. Neither family is a partial family.

On the empty constraint list the partition count has 9 labels and defect 0. The states with only `e0` and only `e1` share the count `(1,0)`. The quotient of that label is defined. The overlapping count separates those two states and merges only `e1` with only `e2`. It has 10 labels and defect 1. The quotient is undefined. Each cover keeps a distinction the other drops. Exactness and separation are different properties of the two maps.

The blocks of the partition share a vertex and no edge. When `e0` and `e3` are the present edges, both blocks are active and the active intersection graph has two vertices and no edge. The same present edges on the overlapping cover produce an edge, because those blocks share carrier edges.

The bare active intersection graph gives the same label to only `e0` and only `e3`. The labelled active-block map keeps the block index and separates them.

One multiply by 3 of `e0` when `e1` is present uses the same partition-count label. The defect is `1/4`. The baseline exactness does not survive that law. This is one table.

These numbers are fixtures. They are not a frozen round.

## Realised overlap

Potential overlap is fixed by the blocks. Realised overlap also requires a present shared edge. `realised_intersection` is the bare graph of the active blocks with that stricter adjacency. `labelled_realised_blocks` keeps the block indices. `realised_overlap_count` counts the present edges in each pairwise intersection. None of the three replaces `active_intersection` or `labelled_active_blocks`.

On the four-edge path, the overlapping family shares two edges. When only the two end edges are present, both blocks are active and the potential graph has an edge. The realised graph has two vertices and no edge. One present shared edge and two present shared edges have the same bare realised graph and different counts.

The blocks of opposite edges on the four-cycle are disjoint. Realised adjacency and potential adjacency are both empty, so those graphs agree. The shared-edge count is the constant 0.

The triangle family `{{(0,1),(1,2)},{(1,2),(0,2)}}` has one possible shared edge. Its realised labelled graph is not the potential labelled graph. Under the empty list the realised labelled graph has 5 labels and defect `1/2`. Under one multiply by 3 of `(0,1)` when `(1,2)` is present it has 5 labels and defect `3/10`. The count of that shared edge has 2 labels and defect 0 under both laws. The guard of that multiply is the shared edge, so the weights are constant on each value of the count. These are fixtures. They are not a frozen round. A block family that changes over time is not one of these maps.

# Definitions for RRC-001

Stage C. These are the meanings the first frozen round uses. Other meanings stay open and are not computed under these names.

## Chosen

**Relational state.** N labelled nodes, `N >= 2`. A state is a simple undirected graph: each unordered pair is present or absent. Pairs are ordered `i < j` lexicographically, as in the Constraint Laboratory. No coordinates are stored.

**Structural size.** For a carrier, structural size is N, the number of nodes. It is not the number of present edges, not the number of blocks, and not a path length.

**Experimenter-designated structure.** A node subset written in the plan. Internal pairs have both ends in the subset. Interface pairs are all the others. A composed pair of structures is two disjoint subsets; hidden pairs are the pairs inside either subset; the interface is the cut. This is an instrument. It is not inferred.

**Open structure definitions, not used in RRC-001.** Connected components of the current graph. Persistent motifs. Symmetry orbits. Behavioural equivalence classes discovered by search rather than declared. A finite external interface found by optimising a statistic. Any of these may name different objects. RRC-001 does not call its subsets by those names.

**Consequential observable, interface items.** The next-step law of the block that contains the current state. The block is the interface bit pattern, or that pattern plus one declared augmentation.

**Consequential observable, propagation items.** The stationary probability that each pair is present, and the stationary probability of toggling that pair in one step. Depth is the smaller endpoint index on the declared path `0—1—…—(N-1)`. That index is a scaffold.

**Strong lumpability.** Every state in a block has the same total probability of moving into each block. The interface process is then Markov for every initial distribution.

**Exact behavioural equivalence, in this round.** Strong lumpability. The defect is the zero rational. A float rendering of that rational is not the test.

**Defect magnitude.** The maximum, over states, of the L1 distance between that state's next-block law and the mean law of its block. Zero if and only if the partition is strongly lumpable. This is not total variation of a stationary marginal, and it is not weak lumpability.

**Approximate equivalence.** Not claimed. A positive defect is a failure of exactness, reported with its rational magnitude. No threshold turns a positive defect into "close enough to equivalent".

**Augmentations.** Refinements of the interface partition by a function of the hidden pairs:

| Name | Extra coordinate |
| --- | --- |
| `interface` | none |
| `edge_count` | number of present hidden pairs |
| `parity` | that number modulo 2 |
| `interface_wedge_counts` | the common-neighbour count of each interface pair |

**Lumpable closure.** The coarsest strong-lumpability refinement of the interface partition obtained by splitting blocks whose states disagree about the next-block law. Its block count is the size of the exact current-state description that still reports the interface. It is computed only when the plan sets `closure` true.

**Recursive composition.** The two-subset partition above, one constructed step from a single subset to two subsets on a shared cut. It is not a discovered hierarchy and it is not six levels of composition.

**Grammar forms the engine may report.**

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `unconstrained_lazy` | The interface is Markov, one step flips at most one interface pair, and every interface pair has the same toggle probability in every block |
| `reweighted_single_toggle` | The interface is Markov and the event shape is unchanged, but the toggle probabilities are not that constant |
| `not_markovian_on_interface` | The event shape still flips at most one pair, and the interface law is not a function of the interface block |
| `outside_grammar` | Some positive-weight step changes more than one interface bit |

A positive defect is `not_markovian_on_interface`, not a transformed grammar. `reweighted_single_toggle` is a transformed weight system with the same event shape. `unconstrained_lazy` is the original unconstrained grammar plus a holding probability.

**Halt.** A state with every weight zero is completed by a self-loop named `halt_self_loop`. The loop is not a relational event.

**Stationary method.** Parity-balanced iteration: the average of a distribution and its image. Tolerance is frozen in the plan. Two starts must agree. A dense solve is required when the state count is at most the plan's dense limit. Disagreement leaves the item `unresolved`. The tolerance is not widened.

## Not chosen

- Weak lumpability.
- Equivalence of stationary marginals as a substitute for lumpability.
- History variables. Hidden pairs are current state.
- An independent hyperedge, or a transition that toggles two pairs.
- Sampling.
- N=7 or larger exhaustive kernels.
- Any identification among six constituent nodes, six edges along a path, six levels of composition, and six units of context.

# Event kernel

Status: typed fixtures. They are not a frozen round and not a scientific cell. The atlas engine stays `rrc-0.4.0`. The method in `src/rrc/event_kernel.py` is `event-kernel-0.1.0`. It is not a new primitive of that engine. No intervention operator is defined. ATLAS-Q15 stays open. EQ-027 is not rerun.

The clock is one declared event. Each event names its source, its target, its kind, and a nonnegative integer weight. Weights that share a source and a target are added. A positive row is divided by its sum with rational arithmetic. A weight of 0 adds nothing. Listing the same events in another order leaves the sums unchanged.

A row with no positive weight is completed by `halt_self_loop`. That self-loop is not an event. A no-op is a declared event whose target is its source. Both records can put probability `1` on the diagonal. The completions stay different.

## Comparison

| Family | State | Declared events | One-step law on the witness | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Single toggle | One row per mask | Flip one named bit | The probability is that bit's weight over the row sum | The existing one-step support |
| Halt row | The same states | No positive weight | Probability `1` on the source, and the completion is `halt_self_loop` | A completion, not an event |
| No-op | The same states | A no-op of positive weight | Probability `1` on the source, and the completion is `noop_event` | An event, including when the probability matches the halt row |
| Summed names | Three states in the witness | Two names for one target, weights `1` and `3`, and a second target of weight `2` | Probabilities `2/3` and `1/3` | The weights add before the division |
| Joint event beside one toggle | Two bits | Flip bit 0, and flip both bits, each of weight `1` | From state 0 the probabilities are `1/2` to state 1 and `1/2` to state 3 | State 3 has Hamming distance 2. It is outside the one-step single-toggle support. Two single toggles can reach it |
| Identified interface | One shared bit | One toggle of weight `1` | Probability `1` to the other state | Ordinary one-bit support |
| Free copies | Two copy bits | One toggle of either copy, weight `1` | From state 0 the probabilities are `1/2` and `1/2` to the two single-copy states | The step leaves the agreement set |
| Coupled copies | Two copy bits | Flip both copies, weight `1` | Probability `1` from state 0 to state 3 | The same shared-bit change as the identified toggle. Hamming distance is 2 |

The single-toggle row is the control. On two bits with every weight equal to `1`, state 0 moves to state 1 or state 2, each with probability `1/2`. State 3 receives probability `0` in that one step.

The joint witness uses the same two bits and the same clock. State 0 moves to state 1 or state 3, each with probability `1/2`. State 3 is the joint flip. The one-step single-toggle successors of state 0 are states 1 and 2. The two laws differ on this state space and this clock. A path of two single toggles still reaches state 3. No universal impossibility is claimed. A larger state that splits the joint step into two microsteps is a different clock or a different state space.

The identified carrier is one bit. Its toggle has probability `1`. The duplicated carrier is two copies of that bit. Agreement is states 0 and 3. The map sends the identified states onto that pair. The coupled update follows the map: identified state 0 goes to identified state 1, and duplicated state 0 goes to duplicated state 3. The free product from state 0 moves to state 1 or state 2 and leaves the agreement set. The map is a bijection of those two state sets. The coupled law matches the identified law on the image. The free-product law does not.

# Event kind and update semantics

Status: typed validation. It is not a frozen round and not a scientific cell. The atlas engine stays `rrc-0.4.0`. `event-kernel-0.1.0` is unchanged. `event-kernel-0.2.0` is a separate method. It is not a new primitive of `rrc-0.4.0`. No intervention operator is defined. Atlas-017 was not rerun.

`kernel` stores `event-kernel-0.1.0`. Its kind check is the old one. A no-op must stay in its source state. A toggle or a joint must change the state. The label is not checked against Hamming distance. A toggle from state 0 to state 3 is accepted. A kind named `transition` is rejected.

`strict_kernel` stores `event-kernel-0.2.0`. The caller passes a bit width or passes none. The function does not infer a bit width from a power-of-two state count.

| Declared width | Kind | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Width `w`, with `n_states = 2^w` | `noop` | Source and target are the same state |
| Width `w` | `toggle` | Hamming distance is exactly one bit |
| Width `w` | `joint` | Hamming distance is at least two bits |
| Width `w` | `transition` | The state changes. The distance is not a claim |
| No width | `noop` | Source and target are the same state |
| No width | `transition` | The state changes. The indices are not bits |
| No width | `toggle` or `joint` | Rejected |

A joint has no smaller cap than the width. Both states already lie in the mask, so the distance is at most `w`. A flip of every bit is a joint when `w` is at least 2. On a one-bit mask every change has distance 1, so a joint is rejected.

A weight of 0 is still parsed. A zero-weight toggle whose distance is not 1 is rejected. A zero-weight toggle whose distance is 1 is kept in the event list and adds no mass. The row then completes by `halt_self_loop` unless some other positive event is present.

Two events with the same source and target add their positive weights. Their kinds stay on the event list. The probability row does not recover the kinds. A joint and a transition can share one probability matrix and remain different records. Duplicate names are rejected. Listing the events in another order leaves the sums unchanged.

The six Atlas-017 catalogues meet these checks. The stored results still say `event-kernel-0.1.0`. The worker item calls `kernel`, not `strict_kernel`. This note adds no ledger row and no equivalence. Typed couplings that call `strict_kernel` are in `docs/coupled-models.md`. They are not a frozen round.

## Item shape

One item is one `(N, rule, partition)` lumpability task, or one `(N, base rule, perturbed rule)` propagation task.

Each item carries its own id, frozen spec, input hash, status, output and receipt. A crash discards only the open item. The watchdog is 120 seconds. The hard ceiling for an ordinary item is five minutes, and the plan must not contain an item whose preflight or estimate exceeds 120 seconds.

`run` accepts `--max-items` and `--budget-seconds` and exits normally when either limit is hit. A long queue is finished by repeated invocations.

## Information value of the first round, before any cell is run

The round is worth running if it can separate these possibilities at small N:

1. Interface reduction is exact for every rule in the grammar.
2. Interface reduction is exact precisely when weights ignore the hidden pairs, and fails as soon as a wedge can sit on a hidden pair (possibly already at N=3).
3. Some intermediate sufficient statistic (count, parity, wedge profile) restores exactness without the full hidden graph.
4. Some N, possibly six, is the first size at which one of these behaviours changes.
5. A local weight change propagates along the declared path index, or it only rescales every rate through the normalising constant.

Any of these, including a null for (4), answers a live question. The round is not justified by the chance that six is special.

## Stopping

If preflight puts every informative N=6 item over 120 seconds, RRC-001 freezes without those items and says so. It does not sample them. If the N≤5 contrasts already separate (1)–(5) as far as this grammar can, a second round still has to name a new question. It is not opened to enlarge N.

# Uniform ge-2 multiply and effective cardinality

Status: scoped identity, checked by `tests/test_count_cardinality.py`. Not a new scientific round. Not a property of every count.

Atlas-006 stored the same count on its five uniform `ge 2` lists. PAT-011 records that observation. Those cells were not rerun. This note proves the count for the family named below, including actions and carriers the round did not use, and records two lists that leave the family.

## Family

The carrier is a simple undirected graph. Its edges are listed in a fixed order. On every carrier edge there is exactly one constraint: multiply by an integer factor `f >= 2`, with action `either`, `form`, or `dissolve`, when at least two other carrier edges that share an endpoint with the event are present. The relation is `ge` and the threshold is 2. The baseline `b` is an integer `>= 1`. No other constraint is present. The composer is `prohibit_then_product`. The kernel is row gcd under `halt_self_loop`. A zero row stays zero. This family has no zero row.

The neighbourhood of an edge is the set used by `incident_neighbour`: every other carrier edge that shares an endpoint. Its size is the degree of that edge in the line graph of the carrier. EQ-014 is a different statement. It counts deadlock states of one prohibit template. It is not used here.

## Statement

Let `W` be the set of carrier edges whose neighbourhood has size at least 2.

Weight-effective cardinality and the raw removal-sensitive count equal `|W|`. The kernel-removal-sensitive count equals `|W|`. Kernel-effective cardinality equals `|W|`, except for one dissolve case named below.

Effective cardinality is the size of a smallest sublist that reproduces the object. The removal-sensitive count is leave-one-out. On the weight table those two counts agree. On the kernel they do not always agree.

## Argument

An edge whose neighbourhood has size 0 or 1 has present-neighbour count at most 1 in every state. The guard never holds. Deleting that constraint leaves every integer weight unchanged, and leaves the reduced kernel unchanged.

An edge `e` in `W` has a state in which its guard holds. For `either` or `form`, place any two neighbours of `e` present and keep `e` absent. For `dissolve`, keep `e` present as well. In that state the column of `e` equals `f*b` under the full list and equals `b` after the constraint on `e` is deleted. The raw tables differ. Every sublist that omits `e` differs from the full table in that column, so the smallest weight sublist is exactly the constraints on `W`. Each of those constraints is removal-sensitive.

The same state separates the kernel from the leave-one-out kernel. Each column is positive. The leave-one-out row agrees with the full row in every column except `e`, where the entries are `b` and `f*b`. Equal positive columns force the two row-gcds to agree, and the column of `e` then forces `f = 1`. That is outside the family. The reduced rows differ. The kernel-removal-sensitive count is `|W|`.

Kernel-effective cardinality can still be smaller than that leave-one-out count. A sublist that omits `e` and keeps any other constraint fails the same gcd comparison in a state where `e` fires and some edge does not. The only remaining candidate is the empty list. The empty list reproduces the kernel exactly when every row is a constant vector: in every state the set of edges whose guards hold is empty or is the entire edge set.

For `either` and for `form`, that constant-row condition fails whenever `W` is nonempty. In the state with exactly two neighbours of a wide edge present and that edge absent, the wide edge fires. Each of those two neighbours has at most one present neighbour, so it does not fire. `form` also refuses a present edge. The row is not constant. The empty list fails. Kernel-effective cardinality equals `|W|`.

For `dissolve`, the constant-row condition can hold. It holds exactly when the carrier's edges are a triangle or a three-edge star. Isolated vertices add no edge and do not change the edge set. In both graphs the line graph is the complete graph on three vertices, every neighbourhood has size 2, and the only state in which any guard holds is the state in which every edge is present. That row is the constant `f*b`. Every other row is the constant `b`. The kernel is the baseline kernel, so kernel-effective cardinality is 0, while `|W|` is 3 and the integer table is not the baseline table. Deleting one of the three constraints makes the full-present row unequal across columns, so the kernel-removal-sensitive count stays 3.

No other simple graph does this. A graph with four or more edges has an edge `e` and two neighbours `a` and `b`. In the state where exactly `e`, `a`, and `b` are present, `e` fires, and any further edge is absent, so that further edge does not fire. The row is not constant. A graph whose edges are not one of those two three-edge graphs, and which still has a narrow edge, produces a non-constant row as soon as one wide edge fires. The two three-edge graphs are the whole exception.

## Where a broader reading stops

A second copy of the same multiply on one edge of a triangle makes the product `f^2` on that edge. Both copies are required, and so are the multiplies on the other two edges. Declared length 4. `|W|` is 3. Effective cardinality and kernel-effective cardinality are 4.

A prohibit with the same guard, added beside the uniform multiplies on a triangle, zeros the prohibited column whenever the guard holds. The multiply on that edge no longer changes the table or the kernel. Effective cardinality stays 3, which is still `|W|`. The failure is the other reading: a constraint whose event lies in `W` can be redundant once the list is not the uniform family.

The `eq 1` template is a different guard. On the three-edge chain, `|W|` for threshold 2 is 1, and the uniform `eq 1` list does not have effective cardinality 1. The check computes that list. It does not execute `plans/atlas-006.json`.

A common-neighbour count is not this neighbourhood. A threshold other than 2, a missing edge, a factor of 1, and any composer other than `prohibit_then_product` are outside the statement. Equality of these cardinalities is not equality of a weight hash with its kernel hash. Occupation is not part of the statement. The identity does not appoint the next round.

# Synchronising composition and sufficient effective descriptions

**Status:** Analytic increment, 26 October 2026.
**Method:** `label-sync-analysis-0.1.0`, analysis only.
**Question:** When can component descriptions be substituted inside a typed
interaction without changing the resulting dynamics?

## 1. Typed inputs, output and clock

A component is a finite nonempty state set S, a fixed handshake alphabet H,
and nonnegative integer matrices W_label on S for finitely many labels.
An entry is the aggregate weight of events with that label, source and target.
Distinct parallel event identities are not preserved by this representation;
their weights add within a label. Labelled self-loops are permitted.

| Feature | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Constituent state | An arbitrary finite state, not necessarily a bit mask |
| Composition input | Two weighted labelled components with the same H |
| Composed state | Cartesian pair `(s,t)`; no extra state beyond the inputs |
| Shared event | Same label in H, both components update, weights multiply |
| Private event | Label outside H, one component updates while the other holds |
| Unmatched shared event | Blocked; an absent matrix is zero |
| Composition output | Another weighted labelled component with the same H |
| Clock | One global composed event, then row normalisation |
| Empty row | Halt self-loop, not an event available to synchronise |
| Reapplication | Defined using the unnormalised output and the same fixed H |

This is synchronization of action labels, not identification of equal interface
states or a changing block-membership operation. The product-of-weights choice
is a declared instrument. It is not asserted to be the canonical policy for
all stochastic systems or a law of physical interaction.

Write the two inputs' label matrices as W_label and V_label. The output is:

```text
label in H:       U_label = W_label tensor V_label
label outside H:  U_label = W_label tensor I + I tensor V_label
```

The label alphabet is the finite union of input labels and H; missing weights
are zero. Sum all U_label matrices and normalise each positive row. A zero row
gets probability one on its own state. Do not insert that completion into the
event matrices before another composition. Private self-loops, in contrast,
are real weighted events and affect the composed event clock.

Raw weights and H are part of the input contract. A component's normalised
Markov kernel is not sufficient input data for this operator. A different
normalisation or synchronization policy would be a different declared operator.

## 2. Iteration and identity

**Associativity at fixed H.** After reassociating Cartesian triples, the two
parenthesisations have equal label matrices before normalisation. For a shared
label, both give `W_label tensor V_label tensor Z_label`. For a private label,
both give the sum of three matrices: that factor's label matrix and identities
in the other two positions. Distributivity proves the equality, including zero
and self-loop matrices. The final normalised kernels therefore also agree.

This proves an iteration property of the specified dynamical operation, not
merely a repeated naming of a tuple. A handshake event of the composed component
can participate in a further joint event with a third component. It requires
all participants under the same H; it is not a model of arbitrary bilateral or
changing synchronization topology. Normalising intermediate outputs and then
reinterpreting probabilities as weights is outside this associativity statement.

**Identity.** The one-state component with one weight-one self-loop for every
label in H, and no private event, is a left and right identity. Its shared
matrices are `[1]` and private matrices `[0]`, giving exactly the other input's
weights. When H is empty, the empty one-state component serves this role.

The all-halt one-state component and this identity both have standalone kernel
`[1]`. For nonempty H they are not interchangeable in composition. A two-state
partner that toggles on a shared label moves with the identity, but halts with
the empty component. Halt completion cannot be promoted to a synchronising event.

## 3. Exact standalone prediction is not a congruence

Let A have states `(z,d)`, with `z,d` each 0 or 1. The hidden coordinate d holds.
The only event flips z, with weight one. Its label is a when d=0 and b when d=1.
Take H={a,b}. Both hidden states give the same aggregate raw weights and the
same normalised law on z: a deterministic flip. The observation dropping d is
strongly lumpable for A, for every starting distribution.

Let B be a two-state component toggling on a with weight one and offering no b.
Retain the observation `(z,B-state)` after composition. From `(z=0,d=0,B=0)`
the composed law moves to observed `(1,1)` with probability one. From
`(z=0,d=1,B=0)` the shared b is blocked and the row halts at observed `(0,0)`.
These sources share their observation but have different outgoing block rows.
There is no exact first-order quotient under that product observation.

The finite checker uses micro encoding `2*z+d` and product encoding `2*micro+B`.
Its witness sources are 0 and 2, both observed as 0. Their block rows are
`[0,0,0,1]` and `[1,0,0,0]`. Nonexact rows are reported as undefined, not filled
with zeros or approximated. This comparison changes label allocation, not the
standalone aggregate raw weights. Ordinary kernel equality and standalone
lumpability have erased information needed by this particular interaction.

## 4. A sufficient quotient rule that does compose

Let pi and rho be surjective observations of the two components. Require, for
every label and every target observation block, that the sum of outgoing label
weights into that block is the same at every source in one source block.
This defines a weighted labelled quotient for each component.

**Preservation theorem.** Under this condition on both inputs, reducing before
composition and composing before reduction have equal labelwise block weights
under `pi times rho`. After normalisation, the product observation is strongly
lumpable and its exact kernel is the kernel of the composed weighted quotients.

**Proof for shared labels.** Sum the product weight over a target product block.
The finite double sum factors into the W_label block sum times the V_label block
sum. Each is fixed by its source observation. Their product is exactly the
shared-label weight in the composition of the quotients.

**Proof for private labels.** The identity on the passive factor sums to one
when the target observation equals the passive source observation, and to zero
otherwise. Each term therefore gives the quotient's label block sum times the
appropriate observed identity. Adding the two private contributions yields the
private-label formula on the quotient product. No block-cardinality multiplier
appears.

**Normalisation and halt.** Summing the equal block weights gives equal row
totals within a source product block. Positive rows normalise identically.
If a total is zero, every source in that block halts at its own observation,
as does the quotient. Thus the exact normalised block rows agree in both cases.

The condition allows hidden state to hold, flip, reset or evolve in other ways.
It constrains labelwise flow into observed blocks, not transitions inside each
block. An event that becomes a quotient self-loop must retain its label and
weight: it can still synchronise with a partner and change that partner's state.
The condition concerns weighted label behaviour, not recovery of all microscopic
event identities or preservation of original carrier meanings.

This is a sufficient rule, not a necessary condition for every particular partner.
For example, if A's a-flip weights are 1 and 2 at the two hidden values, a shared-
only partner still yields a deterministic joint flip. Its product observation
is exact even though the labelwise weights of A differ within a block.

## 5. The private-clock boundary

Add a weight-one private self-loop at every partner state in that last example.
At hidden weight 1, the joint flip and the private event each have probability
`1/2`. At hidden weight 2, they have probabilities `2/3` and `1/3`. The retained
product observation is no longer strongly lumpable. Labels of A have not changed;
its raw weight scale, invisible to its standalone kernel, now matters relative
to the partner's private event.

The contrast follows from the declared product-weight/global-clock convention,
not an invariant assertion about every composition policy. It also shows why
normalised labelled probabilities alone do not generally replace the raw
weighted interface contract. No causal intervention or physical timescale is
inferred from this constructed comparison.

## 6. Verification, scope and precedents

`provenance/label-sync-analysis-check.py` compares sparse event-pair enumeration
with independent dense per-label matrix formulas. Exact Fraction aggregation
checks normalised observations; unit tests also use hand-derived rows. Its
bounded domains and the analytical selection are recorded separately. The
prototype caps itself at 32 states and 2048 event records for cost, not as a
mathematical limit of the proved operator.

Weighted labelled transition systems and the labelwise sum-to-class condition
are established mathematics: see Miculan and Peressotti, *Weak bisimulations for
labelled transition systems weighted over semirings*, Definitions 1–2,
[arXiv:1310.4106](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4106). We use the strong weighted
condition as a sufficient interface contract. Their weak/silent-transition
results are not imported, and the particular product/clock policy here is
explicitly specified rather than attributed to every process algebra.

The proofs are elementary matrix and block-sum consequences, not claims of new
universal theorems. Compared with the previous XOR analysis, the new question
changes the operation and the subsequent system dynamics, and the sufficient
condition permits evolving omitted state. Broad composition, higher-order-state
and ontology questions remain open.

# Incident prohibition and line-graph total domination

Status: scoped identity, checked by `tests/test_domination.py`. Not a new scientific round. Not a property of every grammar.

## Rule

The carrier is a simple undirected graph. Its edges are listed in a fixed order. On every carrier edge `e` there is one constraint: prohibit either toggle of `e` when at least one other carrier edge that shares an endpoint with `e` is present. Baseline is 1. The composer is `prohibit_then_product`. The clock is `halt_self_loop`.

The predicate is `incident_neighbour` with polarity `present`. It reads current presence. A static note that two edges share a vertex is not, by itself, the weight.

## Statement

Let `L` be the line graph of the carrier: one vertex per carrier edge, and an edge of `L` when the two carrier edges share an endpoint.

In state `S`, the weight of event `e` is 0 when the open neighbourhood of `e` in `L` meets `S`, and 1 otherwise. The row of `S` is entirely zero exactly when every vertex of `L` has a neighbour in `S`. That is the definition of a total dominating set of `L`. Members of the set do not dominate themselves.

Under `halt_self_loop` a zero row is completed by a self-loop, so these states are absorbing. The engine counts them as deadlock states.

## Counts checked against an independent enumeration

| Carrier | Line graph | Deadlocks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Three-edge chain | Path on three vertices | 3 |
| Three-edge branch, and a triangle | Complete graph on three vertices | 4 |
| Four-edge cycle | Cycle on four vertices | 9 |
| Two disjoint edges | Two isolated vertices | 0 |
| Two adjacent edges | One edge | 1 |

The two disjoint edges have no total dominating set, because an isolated vertex of `L` has no neighbour. The present-polarity guard on an empty neighbourhood never matches, so those columns stay at baseline and no row is zero. The same count comes from both readings.

The three-edge chain has 3 deadlock states and more than 3 recurrent classes. A recurrent class is not the same object as a total dominating set.

The triangle and the three-edge branch have the same weight table. Their line graphs are the same complete graph on three vertices, and the rule depends on that adjacency only.

Atlas-004 stored deadlock counts for `A4-chain-inc-pro`, `A4-branch-inc-pro`, `A4-cycle-inc-pro`, and `A4-disconnected-inc-pro` agree with this enumeration. Those cells were not rerun.

## Where the identity stops

The deadlock set changes when the template is not on every edge. Dropping one chain constraint leaves a column at baseline, so there is no zero row, while total dominating sets of the full line graph still exist.

A multiply does not write zeros. Polarity `absent` is a different predicate. Action `form` or `dissolve` zeros only one direction. A designated-bit prohibit is not this neighbourhood. Equality of deadlock counts is not equality of weight tables once the line graphs differ.

The identity is not a theorem about occupation, about the incident multiply template, or about any other composer. It does not make domination theory the next round. EQ-014 records it as a method identity.

## Exactness conditions the engine must enforce

For a partition of the finite state space, strong lumpability holds if and only if every state in a block has the same total probability of moving into each block. The one-step interface process is then Markov for every initial distribution, and its transition row is that common row.

The test depends on the original transition and on the partition. It does not depend on a stationary distribution. A stationary distance can be small while lumpability fails, and the engine must not substitute one for the other.

Weights in RRC-001 are non-negative integers. Transition probabilities on a non-halt state are those integers over their sum, as rational numbers. Halt states contribute a self-loop of probability 1 on their own block. Two signatures are equal only when those rationals are equal. There is no rounding in the exactness bit.

Float arithmetic is confined to stationary iteration, where the plan states a tolerance and a second method.

# Four representations of a present line graph

Status: definitions and validation fixtures. No scientific cell is attached to this note. Atlas-008 stored the position-indexed map and is not rerun. The engine string stays `rrc-0.4.0`. The weight compiler is unchanged. The functions are `src/rrc/composition.py`. The checks are `tests/test_composition.py`.

Each map sends a carrier state to a label. The label is a function of the present edges. None of the four adds a coordinate. Exact means strong lumpability of that label under the integer weight table. A positive defect rules out strong lumpability of that partition. It does not rule out every history-dependent description.

## Five operations

A permutation is not one operation. These five are different.

1. A permutation of the original node names that keeps each carrier edge in the same list position. The i-th edge is rewritten with the new names of its endpoints. Which positions share an endpoint does not change.
2. A permutation of positions in the carrier-edge list. The same edges may appear, and the i-th position may now be a different edge.
3. A graph isomorphism. A numbering of the vertices of one simple graph onto another. It need not preserve a fixed carrier, and it need not preserve list positions.
4. An automorphism of a fixed carrier. A numbering of that carrier's vertices that preserves its edge set. The three-edge path has two: the identity and the reversal. An end edge and the middle edge are not in one orbit.
5. A general permutation of edge bits that is not induced by any carrier automorphism. Swapping the middle edge of the three-edge path with one end edge is an example. It permutes toggle coordinates. It is not operation 4.

R2 is unchanged by operation 1 and can change under operation 2. R1 changes under operation 1 and is unchanged by operation 2. R3 follows the isomorphism type of the line graph, which is operation 3. R4 is unchanged by operation 4. Operation 5 is a statement about weight tables and bit coordinates. It is not an automorphism of the carrier, and it is not a renumbering of line-graph vertices.

## R1 — relationship-labelled line graph

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Input | The edges present in one carrier state. |
| Operator | One vertex for each present edge. The vertex name is that edge. Two vertices are adjacent when the edges share an endpoint. Names are sorted, so the carrier edge order does not change the label. |
| Output | An edge-labelled line graph. |
| State | None. |
| Reapplication | Undefined. The vertices are edges, and `line_graph` accepts integer endpoints. No encoding is added in order to apply it again. |
| Recoverability | The vertex names are the present edges, so the present edge set is the label. Given the carrier, the bitset is recovered. The recovery is the retained names. |
| Dynamics | The label separates the carrier states. A partition into singletons is strongly lumpable for every weight table on those states. EQ-022 records that fact. The exactness retains the present edges. |
| Preserved by | Operation 2. Reordering the carrier edge list. The vertex names are the edges, and the names are sorted. |
| Changed by | Operation 1. A permutation of the original node names. This is not a reordering of the edge list. |

The bare line graphs of a triangle and a three-edge star are the same unlabelled graph. The labelled line graphs keep different edge names.

## R2 — position-indexed line graph

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Input | The carrier edge list and one present subset. |
| Operator | `line_graph` of the present edges in carrier order. Vertices are `0 .. k-1` in that order. |
| Output | The bare edge list and the line-graph vertex count. |
| State | None. |
| Reapplication | The static bare line graph accepts `line_graph` again. This observation map does not declare a second label. |
| Recoverability | The bare list does not determine which carrier edges were present. |
| Dynamics | Whatever strong lumpability says for this partition. |
| Preserved by | Operation 1. A node-name permutation that keeps each carrier edge in the same list position. The endpoints of a listed edge move together, so the bare index list is unchanged. |
| Changed by | Operation 2. A permutation of positions in the carrier-edge list. The line-graph vertices are numbered in that list order, so the bare list can change. |

This is the `present_line_graph` map stored by atlas-008.

## R3 — canonical unlabelled line graph

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Input | The bare line graph of the present edges, including isolated line-graph vertices. |
| Operator | The lexicographically least edge list over every numbering of those vertices. Isolated vertices stay in the vertex count. |
| Output | A canonical simple graph. |
| State | None. |
| Reapplication | Defined. The canonical graph is already the least edge list, so the second application returns the same graph. That is idempotence, not a further level. |
| Recoverability | The certificate does not determine the input graph. A triangle and a three-edge star have one certificate. Whitney's exception is that pair among connected simple graphs. It is not a new theorem. |
| Dynamics | The class is an observation of the carrier chain. It is strongly lumpable only when the defect is zero. |
| Preserved by | Any numbering of the line-graph vertices, any order of the carrier edges, and any permutation of the original node labels. |
| Changed by | A change that alters the isomorphism type, or the number of line-graph vertices. |
| Cost | The search enumerates every permutation. It is refused above 8 vertices. The refusal is not a canonical form. An independent backtracking search agrees with the certificate on every simple graph of order 4. |

An ordinary hash of an edge list is not this certificate.

## Canonicalisation is not iteration

Calling the canonicaliser again is not the same operation as building another line graph.

- Canonicalising a graph that is already canonical returns the same edge list. `second_application` is `defined_and_idempotent`. That is idempotence of the numbering.
- Applying `line_graph` to the graph represented by that certificate builds a different graph. The certificate of the three-edge path on four vertices is `[[0,1],[0,2],[1,3]]`, another numbering of that path. Its line graph has three vertices and edges `[[0,1],[0,2]]`. The edge lists differ.
- Iterating the line-graph operator applies that construction again. `iterate_line_graph` records step 0 as the input. One further application of this line graph is a single edge.
- Iterating an observation function would send a label through the same map again. No observation map in this note does that.
- Iterating a dynamical quotient lumps a quotient kernel, when one exists, by a further partition. `successive_observations` does that only when the further label is a function of the previous label and the previous partition is strongly lumpable. Otherwise the next rows stay undefined. That construction is not a second canonicalisation, and it is not a second application of `line_graph`.

A second canonicalisation is the same graph. It is not a new relational level, and it is not evidence that the line-graph operator has been iterated.

## R4 — carrier-automorphism orbit

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Input | A fixed carrier and the present edge set. |
| Operator | The lexicographically least image of that edge set under a vertex permutation that preserves the carrier. The minimum is the sorted edge list, so the carrier's list order does not choose it. |
| Output | One edge subset of the same carrier. |
| State | None. |
| Reapplication | Undefined. The automorphism group belongs to the carrier, and the representative does not determine that carrier. |
| Recoverability | The representative is one member of the orbit. The orbit does not determine which member was present. |
| Dynamics | Under an empty constraint list, a positive integer baseline, and `halt_self_loop`, the baseline kernel commutes with the carrier automorphisms. The orbit partition of a group-equivariant chain is strongly lumpable. EQ-023 records that application. A constraint that breaks the symmetry is outside it. |
| Preserved by | Carrier automorphisms, and reordering the carrier edge list. |
| Changed by | A node permutation that is not an automorphism of the carrier. The integer coordinates of the representative move. |
| Cost | The same cap of 8 vertices. Above the cap the search is refused. |

R4 is not the unlabelled isomorphism class of the present graph, and it is not R3. An end edge and a near-centre edge of a path are isomorphic as graphs. They are different orbits of the path.

## Four-cycle baseline, recomputed

The carrier is the four-cycle with edges `(0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (0,3)`, empty constraints, baseline 1. The fixture recomputes the maps. Atlas-008 already stored the position-indexed cell: 8 labels, defect `1/2`. The degree cell stored there has 6 labels and defect 0. Those files were not rewritten.

| Representation | Labels | Defect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R2 position-indexed line graph | 8 | `1/2` |
| R3 canonical line graph | 6 | 0 |
| R4 carrier orbit | 6 | 0 |
| Degree sequence | 6 | 0 |
| Edge count | 5 | 0 |

R3, R4, and the degree sequence are one partition on this carrier. The edge count is coarser: it merges the two-edge states that are a path with the two-edge states that are a matching. R2 is finer than R3. Two present graphs whose line graphs are the same path on three vertices can have different position-indexed edge lists. The witness in the fixture is the present edges `{0,2,3}` and `{0,1,2}`.

The quotient kernel of R3 is stored by the fixture as exact fractions. From the empty graph the next class is the one-edge class, with probability 1. From one edge the next class is empty with probability `1/4`, an adjacent pair with probability `1/2`, and an opposite pair with probability `1/4`. From either two-edge class the next class is one edge or three edges, each with probability `1/2`. From three edges the next class is an adjacent pair with probability `1/2`, an opposite pair with probability `1/4`, and the full cycle with probability `1/4`. From the full cycle the next class is three edges, with probability 1.

## Where the same baseline separates the maps

On the triangle and on the three-edge star, R2, R3, R4, the degree sequence, and the edge count are one partition. Each is exact. Those carriers are the controls where the representations agree.

On the three-edge chain, R2, R3, and the degree sequence are one partition, with 5 labels and defect `4/9`. R4 has 6 labels and is exact. The canonical line graph merges an end edge with the middle edge. Those two states have different next-orbit laws. The carrier reversal keeps them apart.

On the four-edge path, R3 and the degree sequence are one partition, with 7 labels and defect `1/3`. R2 has 8 labels and the same defect. The partitions differ. The shared defect does not identify the maps. R4 has 10 labels and is exact. EQ-023 covers that exactness. It does not cover the defect of R2 or R3.

## One constraint outside EQ-023

The same four-cycle, with one multiply by 3 of edge `(0,1)` when edge `(1,2)` is present, uses the same R4 partition. The defect is `11/24`. The quotient is undefined. The orbit label does not stay exact after the law stops commuting with the carrier automorphisms. This is one table, not a census of constraints.

# A shared port that changes: dynamics, consistency and later participation

**Status:** Analytical increment, 26 October 2026.
**Method:** `shared-port-analysis-0.1.0`, analysis-only.

A changing interface can be shared state without being an additional independent
coordinate. Here components identify a port value already read from their own
states. Their composite retains that boundary and supports further composition.
Agreement is a transition constraint: synchronizing equal labels alone does not
guarantee it. This is one declared operator, not a canonical rule for all gluing.

## 1. Typed objects and event clock

Fix a finite nonempty port set P and a finite handshake alphabet H, possibly
empty. A component consists of finite nonempty states S, an onto boundary map
`b:S -> P`, and finite nonnegative integer label matrices W_l. Positive entries
are aggregate event weights; duplicate events of one label add. Individual
event identities are not recovered from these matrices.

Require **private port preservation**: for l outside H, `W_l(s,u)>0` implies
`b(s)=b(u)`. Shared events may change the port. A zero-weight entry is not a
positive write; invalid endpoints are still invalid. Surjectivity is a typing
choice ensuring nonempty compatible fibres, not a reachability assertion.

| Aspect | Declared contract |
| --- | --- |
| Identified composite state | `(s,t)` with `b_A(s)=b_B(t)` |
| Port value | Their common value; no extra coordinate is appended |
| Shared label h | Pair two h events with product weight; keep only compatible targets |
| Private label | One component updates and the other holds; private writes preserve the port |
| Output boundary | The inherited common port, with the same P and H |
| Normalisation | Only the final admitted event row; keep intermediate weights raw |
| Empty admitted row | Implicit halt self-loop, not a real event |
| Reapplication | The output is another component of this same type |

The value of the interface can change. The port type P, ownership rule and H
remain fixed. This is not evolving membership, changing handshake topology,
independently added controller state or identification of all constituent states.

## 2. Definition and well-typed output

For components A and B write `S times_P T` for their compatible pairs. For
compatible source `(s,t)` and target `(u,v)`, define raw output matrices:

```text
h in H:       U_h((s,t),(u,v)) = W_h(s,u) * V_h(t,v)
l outside H: U_l((s,t),(u,v)) = W_l(s,u) * indicator(t=v)
                                + indicator(s=u) * V_l(t,v)
```

Absent matrices are zero. These are the previous Cartesian weighted-label
formulas restricted to compatible sources **and targets**. Filtering before
normalisation is part of the new instrument. It must not be mistaken for a
proof that agreement was invariant in the unconstrained copy system.

Each port fibre is nonempty in both inputs, so their fibre product is nonempty
and its boundary onto P. A positive private output event changes only one
input, whose port is preserved. Thus the output satisfies the private contract
and can participate in another shared-port product. No engine method is changed.

## 3. Reapplication, associativity and unit

**Associativity theorem.** For three such components at fixed P and H, the
canonical reassociation `((s,t),r) <-> (s,(t,r))` is a boundary-preserving equality
of raw labelled weights on triples whose three source ports agree.

For a shared h, either parenthesization keeps precisely target triples whose
three ports agree, with weight `W_h(s,u)*V_h(t,v)*Z_h(r,w)`. An incompatible
intermediate pair could not be part of a compatible final triple. For a private
label, the result is the sum of the three single-factor updates, with the other
two states held fixed. Each private write preserves the common port. This is
the same sum under both parenthesizations; no fibre-size factor appears.
These equalities prove the raw dynamical claim, not only a set identity.
The final normalized kernels also agree. Intermediate normalisation followed
by interpreting probabilities as weights is outside this theorem.

**Unit.** Take states P with identity boundary, one weight-one shared h event
`p -> q` for every h and every pair of port values, and no private events.
The bijection `(s,b(s)) -> s` (or its left-sided version) preserves all raw
labels and weights. For each shared event there is exactly one unit transition
with the required source and target port, of weight one. Private events pair
with the fixed matching unit state and preserve its value. This proves both
identity laws. The unit relays arbitrary shared port changes; it is not a
one-state halt component, and its standalone normalised law need not be inert.
Its identity property is for the identified operator. With unconstrained
Cartesian copies, its different possible target ports can leak out of agreement;
being this operator's unit does not imply that separate copies stay consistent.

The private-write contract matters. If an input could privately change p to q,
the other unit state would hold p; filtering would suppress that write, so this
unit would not preserve the input. Other ownership/update rules may admit such
writes, but they define other operators. When P is a singleton this construction
reduces exactly to the previously declared Cartesian product and its unit.

These are finite weighted-automaton facts under a common boundary, not a claim
that every adaptive interface is associative or that a hierarchy must emerge.

## 4. When do synchronized copies already agree?

Let F be the **unfiltered Cartesian** synchronization product with the same raw
input weights and H. Let I be its agreement image `b_A(s)=b_B(t)`.

**Invariance criterion.** I is invariant under F's final kernel if and only if,
for every shared h and every compatible source `(s,t)`, every positive pair of
h events `s -> u`, `t -> v` has `b_A(u)=b_B(v)`.

Private events cannot leave I by their contract. A shared event leaves I exactly
when its two positive target ports disagree. Nonnegative weights cannot cancel
such a contribution; normalization preserves positivity. An empty Cartesian
row halts within I. These observations prove both directions.

When the criterion holds, the inclusion of identified states into I preserves
raw labelled weights and is a kernel conjugacy onto an invariant image. It is
an **injective image comparison**, not a noninjective lumpability claim or a
carrier automorphism. Outside I, the copy system can have other states/dynamics.

Without invariance, identified raw matrices still equal the I-by-I restriction,
but their normalized rows need not be the original kernel's restricted rows:

| Raw row | Relationship to the Cartesian kernel |
| --- | --- |
| Some admitted weight remains | The identified row is its one-step law conditioned on the next state lying in I |
| Original raw total is zero | Both systems halt at the valid source |
| Original total positive, admitted total zero | Conditioning has zero probability and is undefined; the new operator halts by its declared completion |

For the first case, if total raw mass is T and admitted mass R>0, retained
Cartesian probabilities are admitted weights divided by T. Dividing again by
`R/T` gives weights divided by R, exactly the identified row. This is a rowwise
conditioning identity, not a claim about conditioning an entire future path.

An h write `0 -> 1` of weight 2 paired with an h hold `0 -> 0` of weight 3
leaves agreement with weight 6. A private unit hold provides admitted weight 1.
The copy kernel leaks `6/7`; the identified row holds with probability 1. Remove
that private event and conditioning is undefined, while the identified row
halts. Undefined restricted/conditional laws are left absent in the evidence.

### Equal marginals are not a shared random choice

Give each two-port component one h event into port 0 of weight 1 and into port
1 of weight 2, from either source. Both have the same port kernel `[1/3,2/3]`.
Their Cartesian pairing has weights 1,2,2,4 on target pairs 00,01,10,11. It
leaks `4/9` from each agreement state. Enforcing agreement leaves weights 1 and
4, so the identified port law is `[1/5,4/5]`, not either original marginal.
Identical marginal laws did not provide a common random draw. A different
correlated coupling would require a different declared matching/weight rule.

The clock policy is consequential. If rejected Cartesian attempts are counted
as holds at their source instead of discarded, the port rows in this example
become `[5/9,4/9]` and `[1/9,8/9]`. The checker reports this as an explicit
alternate-clock control. It is not the shared-port operator or an observation
of physical duration. No inequivalence caused by this policy is attributed to
spontaneously discovered relational structure.

## 5. A dynamic, consequential and reducible interface

Let A have states `(x,p)`, B have `(p,y)`, with all three variables binary.
Each shared h event flips its local p copy with weight one. A privately flips
x with weight `1+p`; B privately flips y with weight one. In the composite the
single identified p changes on h and affects the x rate. No new independent
interface variable is appended: there are eight `(x,p,y)` states, rather than
sixteen Cartesian states storing both copies.

The input state declarations already allow p to vary independently of x and y:
all `(x,p)` and `(p,y)` combinations are specified. That independence enters in
the inputs. Identification removes one redundant copy; it does not create p
from an overlap, grouping or a name assigned to a collection.

The copy agreement image is invariant here. The identified dynamics are exactly
ordinary current-state single-coordinate flips on the three-bit encoding:
`x` has weight `1+p`, `p` weight 1 and `y` weight 1. The x rate is a literal
factor-2 multiply when p is present. This **particular construction** therefore
reduces to the existing positive single-toggle grammar; it is not a new engine
primitive. Arbitrary shared-port components need not admit this bit encoding.

Observe only `(x,y)`. At x=y=0, p=0 gives block row
`[1/3,1/3,1/3,0]`; p=1 gives `[1/4,1/4,1/2,0]`, in observed order 00,01,10,11.
The observation is not strongly lumpable. The interface evolves and is
predictively consequential under this rate choice, rather than merely renamed.

As a null, set the x weight to one at both p values, keeping h and y events.
The same observation becomes exact even though p still changes. Thus a changing
shared port does not automatically matter for every predictive task.

## 6. Closed prediction versus an inherited interface

For any surjective observation `pi:S -> Q`, an inherited boundary `b_hat:Q -> P`
with `b=b_hat compose pi` exists **if and only if** b is constant on pi blocks.
Necessity follows by evaluating b_hat on one observed value. For sufficiency,
define b_hat(q) using any state in that block; constancy makes it well-defined.
It is unique and onto because pi and b are onto. This is elementary map
factorization, not an additional stochastic theorem.

In the no-feedback null above, `(x,y)` has a closed Markov law but merges p=0
with p=1. It therefore has no inherited port map to the original P and cannot
be substituted as the same port-typed component just from that kernel.
Appending a fresh port or changing its meaning would be an explicit new model
choice. Conversely, preserving b alone does not ensure a closed law: hidden
rates inside one port fibre can still destroy lumpability.

This is a type boundary, separate from the earlier all-partner criterion for
unconstrained Cartesian states. That theorem cannot silently be imported into
this identified-state context class. No minimal abstraction for all interfaces,
histories, observations or policies is classified here.

## 7. Verification, precedents and limits

The state set is a conventional fibre product of finite sets; weighted
synchronization, support invariance, conditioning and map factorization are
established mathematics. The RRC-specific increment specifies one compatible
dynamical gluing rule, proves its reapplication laws and exposes the distinction
between prediction and retaining a usable boundary.

Related precedent includes Baez, Fong and Pollard,
[*A Compositional Framework for Markov Processes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.06448),
which composes open continuous-time processes through inputs/outputs, and Baez
and Courser, [*Coarse-Graining Open Markov Processes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.11343),
which studies coarse-graining with that composition. Those boundary-state,
continuous-time and steady-state constructions are different from the present
port-value fibre product and row-normalized event rule. Their categorical
results are not claimed as a proof of this operator's laws or an identification
with our process. No universal mathematical novelty is asserted.

`provenance/shared-port-analysis-check.py` compares sparse event matching with
dense Cartesian label matrices restricted by an explicit image, checks exact
Fraction rows against the support criterion, and compares the feedback model
with a separate bit-table construction. Tests add hand fractions and previous
sparse-Cartesian compatibility. The bounded domain was predeclared separately;
general claims follow from the proofs, not its fixture counts. Software caps
(64 Cartesian validation states, 4096 event records) are not theorem bounds.

The port type and handshake alphabet do not evolve, and no independent
membership/controller state, causal intervention, autonomous entity, physical
clock or RS ontology is derived. Frozen history and old methods remain intact;
this analytical increment adds zero scientific workers or adopted atlas cells.

| Permitted relabelling | Swapping the two pair bits preserves the count. The geometric names move: bit 0 named `(0,1)` becomes the bit named `(1,2)`. A permutation is an equivalence of a weight table only when the events and the weights move with the bits. The count witness has no weight table. |
| Recoverability | The count is not injective. Masks 1 and 2 both have count 1. |

## Extended state

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Input | Three listed bits `(pair0, pair1, activity)`. |

| Classification | `reducible_to_listed_bit`. |

Both of the following hold. They are different claims. Relative to the two pair bits, states 1 and 5 share the projected mask and differ in the third coordinate. Relative to the three listed bits, the activity table is ordinary pair state. EQ-027 records the second claim for this table. A freely toggling third bit, with every weight equal to 1, gives the same pair-toggle probability at both values of that bit. That free bit is not a witness of interaction.

## Joint event

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Input | The same three-bit state as the extended family. |
| Output | A proposed next state. |
| State | Unchanged. The step does not add a bit. |
| Transition law | No current-state weight on the one-step single-toggle support assigns this step a positive probability. |
| Event support | The permitted support in this scope is one bit flip in one step. |
| Constraints | None added. |
| Permitted relabelling | A bit permutation preserves Hamming distance. |
| Recoverability | The target is a state of the same 8-element space. |
| Further composition | Two successive single toggles are the existing clock, applied twice. |
| Classification | `outside_one_step_single_toggle`. |

From state 0 the one-step successors are states 1, 2, and 4. State 5 flips bit 0 and bit 2 together. The Hamming distance is 2, so state 5 is not a one-step successor. The paths `0 → 1 → 5` and `0 → 4 → 5` each use two single toggles. An extra intermediate state, or a clock that observes only every second toggle, can carry the same pair of bit changes. This scope is the same three-bit state, the one-step clock, and the single-toggle support. No universal impossibility is claimed. History at an unchanged current state is a different gate failure and is not given an engine change.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Input | Edges `(0,1)`, `(1,2)`, `(2,3)`. |
| Output | One carrier state of 3 bits. There are 8 states. |
| State | Listed pair state. |

| Event support | One-bit toggles. |
| Constraints | None in this witness. |

| Recoverability | Each edge is one bit of the state. |

The shared edge `(1,2)` occurs once. A toggle of that edge is one event.

## Duplicated interface

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Input | Four bits: `(0,1)`, copy A of `(1,2)`, copy B of `(1,2)`, and `(2,3)`. |
| Output | One product state of 4 bits. There are 16 states. |
| State | Listed pair state of those four bits. |

| Event support | One-bit toggles on the free product. |
| Constraints | Agreement of the two copies is the subset in which copy A equals copy B. That subset has 8 states. It is not an extra bit. |
| Permitted relabelling | Swapping the two copy bits preserves agreement. |
| Recoverability | On an agreement state, either copy and the two outer bits recover the identified 3-bit state. |

Toggling both copies stays in the agreement set and has Hamming distance 2. From state 0 that coupled update lands on state 6, which is not a one-step successor of the 4-bit free product.
